name: Score across the activation spectrum
summary: A line chart scoring how well a unit's interpretation holds in each band of its own activation range, from weakest firings to maximum, with autoencoder features and raw MLP neurons on the same axes. It exists to test whether interpretability survives outside the top-activating examples.
explanation:
### Why this chart and not another

The section already has its headline number: a blinded annotator scoring features and MLP neurons on a rubric, one total per unit ([[manual-interpretability-scoring|manual human analysis]]). That format cannot answer the question 4.1.4 raises. An interpretation is one claim about a unit that fires at many strengths, and it is usually formed by reading the top-activating examples. The paper says plainly this flatters [[polysemanticity|polysemantic]] units — many look clean at their maximum and fall apart lower down ([[max-dataset-example-bias|the maximal-example weakness]]). A bar, a mean, or a histogram of totals averages over exactly the axis where that failure would show, so none can rule it out.

The activation range therefore has to become an axis. A table of eleven per-band means would carry the numbers and lose the claim, which is about shape: where the score climbs, how sharply, and whether the series stay apart. Drawing [[feature|features]] and neurons together does what a features-only plot could not — neurons climb too, which places the rise on firing hard rather than on the dictionary.

### How to read it, step by step

The x axis is the [[activation-interval|activation interval]]: each unit's range from zero to its own maximum, cut into eleven bands, with examples sampled uniformly from each so weak firings get looked at as often as strong ones. The labels `~0%` to `~100%` are fractions of *that unit's own peak*, never an absolute activation. That normalisation lets a feature peaking at $9$ and one peaking at $0.6$ share a column, and is why nothing here compares across units in raw magnitude.

The y axis is one item of the [[feature-interpretability-rubric|interpretability rubric]], scored $0$ to $5$. The order matters: the annotator forms a single interpretation from the whole spectrum first, then scores each band against it. So a low score does not say the band is confusing on its own — it says the band disagrees with the one story committed to for the unit.

Colour is unit type: magenta for [[sparse-autoencoder|autoencoder]] features, teal for the transformer's own [[neuron-notation|MLP neurons]], scored [[blinded-annotation|without the annotator knowing which]]. The faded dots are individual scored intervals at whole-number scores, darker where more stacked up. The lines are per-band means — $412$ intervals across $162$ units, roughly $37$ a band, so single-band wobbles are noise. Look first at the dotted line at $3$ and where each curve meets it; its own label calls it *subjective*, an impression rather than a derived cutoff.

### What a bad result would look like

The blunt failure is magenta lying on teal, or converging with it at the top: dictionary learning buying nothing the neuron basis did not already have. The instructive failure is magenta near $5$ at the top falling off a cliff by `~60%` — features looking [[monosemanticity|monosemantic]] only through the lens this analysis distrusts.

Neither happens, and neither does the strong result. Magenta above $3$ everywhere would mean the interpretation covers the whole range; instead it starts near $2.6$ and crosses around `~20%`. The paper offers no confident account of that low end, only that a direction learned [[feature-at-slight-angle|at a slight angle]] to the true one would misbehave there. Two checks of your own: move the threshold to $4$ and the crossing slides to roughly `~40%`, so the vertical gap is sturdier evidence than the crossing point; and read the dot cloud, since a mean of $2.6$ split between $5$ and $0$ would describe no unit at all.

### Where it comes back

This exact shape appears once; its parts recur. Read it against the rubric histogram — same annotator, same scoring collapsed to one total per unit. That plot sizes the feature–neuron gap; this one says where along the spectrum the gap lives. The case-study [[feature-activation-distribution-plot|activation distributions]] ask a related question with a [[computational-proxy|computational proxy]] instead of a human, and drift the same way.

The soft low end is the admitted weak point: [[low-interval-activation-skew|most real activations are small]], so most land in the worst-scoring bands. The paper's answer is the [[expected-value-plot|activation-mass]] argument — [[large-activations-dominate|large activations carry most of the effect]] on the output — which shifts the question rather than closing it.
